subtitle: People process information in different ways, and neuroinclusive leaders design work with that in mind. You will learn to keep expectations clear while keeping individual support private.
scope: For leaders improving team practices across recruitment, supervision, and development. Neurodivergent people have varied strengths and needs; this course does not diagnose staff, determine disability eligibility, or authorize accommodation decisions. Use current HR and ADA procedures for individual requests. Course participation and personal disclosure are separate choices.
introTranscript: Neuroinclusive leadership examines how work is organized, communicated, and evaluated. It does not ask leaders to identify which employees are neurodivergent or assume that a diagnostic label predicts a person’s strengths. This course follows a practice policy-analysis team that changes how it assigns work, conducts meetings, gives feedback, and offers development. Leaders practice separating the essential result from a familiar method, improving shared conditions, responding to individual requests through the proper process, and checking whether a change actually helped. Clear expectations and flexibility can support each other when the work and the reason for a change are well understood.

intro.heading: Recognize variation without sorting people
intro.body:
People can differ in how they process spoken information, manage interruptions, interpret social cues, or respond to sensory conditions. Neurodiversity is a way to recognize that variation. It is not a list of abilities that every person with a particular diagnosis shares. A leader cannot reliably identify a person’s needs from eye contact, speaking pace, or preference for written information.

In a practice policy team, an analyst provides careful written comments but rarely speaks first in meetings. That observation does not establish disengagement or a diagnosis. A useful question is whether the team’s decision process gives the analyst a timely way to contribute relevant knowledge.

Invite discussion of ordinary work conditions: which instructions are clear, where interruptions occur, and how people can prepare. Staff should not have to disclose a diagnosis to explain that an agenda helps them contribute. Individual accommodation requests still need the proper process; a general team conversation cannot make those decisions.

lessons.keyStatement: Understand the work experience without classifying the person.

flashcards.back: Variation in how people think, learn, process information, and experience the world. It describes human variation, not a performance rating.
A term some people use for ways of thinking or processing that differ from commonly expected patterns. Do not assign the label to a colleague.
A fundamental duty of a position, confirmed through the appropriate job and HR process.
A person’s preferred way of working; it is not by itself a diagnosis or a determination about accommodation.
An individualized change considered through the authorized process to support equal employment opportunity.
Changes to ordinary team practices, such as clearer instructions, that do not require staff to disclose personal health information.

items.title: Observation
items.body: Describe what actually happened before interpreting it. The analyst contributed an accurate written comment after a fast meeting. That tells you about the timing and form of participation. It does not establish why the analyst was quiet or whether the person has a disability.

items.title: Variation
items.body: People with the same diagnostic label can have different needs and preferences. Even a well-intended strength stereotype can narrow assignments. In the policy team, do not reserve every detailed task for someone presumed to be neurodivergent; ask about skills and assess the relevant work.

items.title: Invitation
items.body: Ask about helpful work conditions in a way that allows anyone to respond. For example, invite suggestions about agenda timing and written input. Do not ask staff to identify a diagnosis in a group discussion or make personal disclosure the price of receiving a usable process.

tabs.label: Label first
tabs.body: Starting with a presumed label may feel like personalization, but it makes the leader’s assumption the basis for action. It can also expose or mischaracterize someone. Start with the task, observed condition, and the person’s account of what would help.

tabs.label: Work first
tabs.body: Starting with the work lets the leader examine participation, clarity, and relevant evidence without diagnosing anyone. It supports a practical change such as an earlier agenda. It does not remove the need to coordinate an individual accommodation request when one is raised.

tabs.label: Strength stereotype
tabs.body: Assuming every neurodivergent employee is unusually analytical sounds positive. It can still restrict opportunity and ignore individual interests. Assign analysis or presentation work from demonstrated skills and development goals rather than a presumed group strength.

check.question: What does the analyst’s quiet participation establish?
check.correct: A work observation that invites examination of meeting conditions, not a diagnosis.
wrong: Proof that the analyst is disengaged.
A reason to assign only solitary work.
check.feedbackCorrect: An observable participation pattern can guide a process question without becoming a personal diagnosis.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Quiet participation may be easy to interpret through familiar expectations, but neither disengagement nor diagnosis follows from it. Restricting assignments compounds the assumption. Examine when and how useful contributions reach the decision, then ask about usable work conditions.

items.text: The analyst submitted an accurate written comment.
The meeting ended before written comments were read.
Could an earlier agenda support preparation?
How can written input reach the decision?
Quietness proves a diagnostic condition.
All people with that condition prefer solitary work.

responses: The diagnosis is unsupported and may misdirect the change.
This examines the actual work while protecting personal choice.

lessons.transfer: Identify one work observation and rewrite its interpretation as a process question.

move.control: You can examine how contributions enter decisions.
move.failure: An observation becomes a personal label that limits opportunity.

lessons.title: Separate the result from the familiar method
lessons.summary: Identify the essential result in a sample policy-analysis task.
lessons.objective: Identify the essential result in a sample policy-analysis task.
objectives: Identify the essential result in a sample policy-analysis task.
Distinguish a job requirement from a habitual work method.
Propose a method change while preserving relevant standards and authority.
takeaways: Name the required result before defending a method.
Check whether a format measures the actual work.
Coordinate formal changes while retaining relevant standards.
lessons.statement: A familiar method is not automatically an essential requirement.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Separate the result from the familiar method
intro.body:
A team may confuse the work it needs with the method it usually uses. A rapid verbal briefing, constant availability in chat, or an open office may be customary. Whether any of those is essential to a particular position requires a job-related examination through the appropriate process. Neuroinclusive leadership starts by making that distinction visible.

The practice policy team needs an accurate comparison of service options, clear limitations, and timely recommendations. Requiring every analyst to explain all findings without notes in an unannounced meeting may measure performance under surprise conditions more than the quality of the analysis. A written summary followed by questions could provide different and more relevant evidence.

Do not remove an essential function or alter a formal requirement independently. Describe the desired result, the barrier introduced by the method, and the proposed alternative for review. Flexibility has a purpose: enabling the actual work, not declaring that deadlines, accuracy, or accountability no longer matter.

Distinguish a job requirement from a habitual work method.
Propose a method change while preserving relevant standards and authority.
What should the leader examine first?
lessons.keyStatement: A familiar method is not automatically an essential requirement.

items.title: Result
items.body: State what must be accomplished in concrete terms. For the policy comparison, the result is a supported recommendation delivered by the agreed date. If the team instead describes the requirement as “sound confident in a surprise briefing,” ask which part actually establishes the quality of the decision support.

items.title: Method
items.body: A work method is how the task is performed. Some methods are genuinely necessary; others reflect habit. For example, simultaneous conversation may suit a quick clarification but obstruct careful comparison of figures. Examine the task before treating one communication format as the only acceptable way to contribute.

items.title: Authority
items.body: Confirm essential functions and formal conditions with the people or areas responsible. A leader can prepare a proposed change, but should not invent a legal conclusion about accommodation or unilaterally revise a classified position. Explain what the alternative preserves and what question needs authorized review.

tabs.label: Same format
tabs.body: An identical format is easy to administer and compare, but can include demands unrelated to the required result. It may give the appearance of fairness without useful job evidence. Check what the format measures before relying on its score.

tabs.label: Relevant flexibility
tabs.body: A different method can preserve accuracy, timeliness, and the essential function while reducing a barrier. Its value depends on effectiveness. A written comparison is useful when it reveals the analysis; it would not replace an essential live interaction without appropriate review.

tabs.label: No standards
tabs.body: Removing all expectations avoids difficult conversations in the short term but does not support the work or the employee. Keep relevant standards clear and coordinate the conditions needed to meet them. Inclusion is not a reason to leave performance unexplained.

check.question: What should guide a proposed briefing change?
check.correct: The required work result, relevant standards, and authorized review of the alternative.
wrong: The manager’s preference for spontaneous speaking.
A decision to remove every deadline.
A presumed diagnosis that replaces job evidence.
check.feedbackCorrect: The change must support the essential work rather than simply replace one preference with another.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Spontaneous speaking may be familiar but is not automatically the essential result. Removing deadlines abandons a relevant question instead of resolving access, and a diagnosis cannot substitute for task evidence. Name the result and review how an alternative would achieve it.

items.text: The comparison identifies material evidence limits.
The report is ready by the agreed decision date.
Every answer must be spoken without notes.
All analysis must happen in a noisy shared space.
Confirm a position’s essential functions with HR.
Route an individual accommodation request.

scenario.prompt: What should the leader examine first?
options: What the job requires and whether the briefing method provides relevant evidence.
responses: A personal impression does not define the required work.
This connects the assessment to its real purpose.
Evaluation is still needed; its relevance and conditions need attention.

lessons.transfer: Map one task to its result, current method, possible barrier, and authorized alternative.

move.control: You can question whether a method serves the required result.
move.failure: A habitual format is defended as essential without examination.

lessons.title: Make instructions, priorities, and changes usable
lessons.summary: Rewrite an ambiguous assignment with deliverables and priorities.
lessons.objective: Rewrite an ambiguous assignment with deliverables and priorities.
objectives: Rewrite an ambiguous assignment with deliverables and priorities.
Plan a predictable way to communicate a change in work.
Distinguish a shared clarity improvement from an individual accommodation decision.
takeaways: Make priorities and completion expectations visible.
Explain changes instead of relying on staff to infer them.
Use shared clarity while preserving individual support processes.
lessons.statement: Clear work design reduces the need to guess.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Make instructions, priorities, and changes usable
intro.body:
Ambiguous instructions can create avoidable effort for any employee. A request to “handle this soon” leaves the recipient to infer the deadline, expected depth, and priority relative to other tasks. Leaders can make these conditions clearer without asking anyone to disclose a disability. Predictability means explaining the work, not promising that public-service priorities will never change.

In the practice policy team, an analyst receives three urgent requests from different managers. The analyst starts the longest one while the team expects a short response first. A shared priority list, named decision maker, and clear definition of completion can prevent the mismatch.

When priorities change, explain what changed, which task moves, and where questions can be raised. Avoid using a shared checklist as proof that every individual need has been met. A person may still need a different arrangement through the accommodation process; clarity helps the team but is not a universal solution.

inThisLesson: Rewrite an ambiguous assignment with deliverables and priorities.
Plan a predictable way to communicate a change in work.
Distinguish a shared clarity improvement from an individual accommodation decision.
What change addresses the problem?
lessons.keyStatement: Clear work design reduces the need to guess.

items.title: Instruction
items.body: Specify the output, purpose, due date, relevant standard, and a contact for questions. For the short policy response, state that the team needs a one-page comparison of two options by Thursday. This lets the analyst plan the actual task rather than infer the manager’s unstated expectation.

items.title: Priority
items.body: Competing assignments need an agreed order and someone authorized to resolve conflicts. If two managers both say “urgent,” asking the employee to work out the hierarchy alone shifts a management responsibility. A visible priority decision makes trade-offs explicit without requiring the employee to justify a diagnosis.

items.title: Change
items.body: A changed deadline affects the plan even when the change is necessary. Explain which work can pause and confirm that the revised instruction was received. In the policy team, announcing a new deadline only during a noisy corridor conversation creates a preventable information gap.

tabs.label: Implied expectations
tabs.body: Implied instructions are quick for a manager who already knows the context. They transfer interpretation work to the employee and can produce inconsistent results. A short written clarification often saves time otherwise spent correcting a misunderstood deliverable.

tabs.label: Usable structure
tabs.body: A visible task list and clear completion standard help staff plan and ask focused questions. They should remain proportionate to the work. Too many detailed instructions can obscure the priority, so distinguish essential information from optional background.

tabs.label: Rigid predictability
tabs.body: Treating predictability as a promise of no change is unrealistic in public service. The useful commitment is to explain changes and their consequences. That allows necessary flexibility without making employees discover revised priorities only after work is judged late.

check.question: Which assignment gives a usable starting point?
check.correct: A defined output, purpose, priority, deadline, and question route.
wrong: “Handle it soon” with no priority decision.
Three conflicting urgent instructions left for the employee to reconcile.
A checklist declared sufficient for every individual need.
check.feedbackCorrect: The instruction makes the work and coordination needs explicit without assuming one solution fits everyone.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Brief instructions are not necessarily clear. “Soon” and competing urgent demands leave the important decisions unstated. A checklist can help, but cannot establish that every individual need is met. Define the assignment and preserve a route for questions and support.

items.text: Provide a one-page comparison by Thursday.
Identify the decision and evidence the report supports.
The manager confirms which of two tasks goes first.
The new deadline includes a decision about paused work.
The deadline exists only in the manager’s mind.
The employee is judged on an unstated page limit.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Three managers give an analyst competing urgent assignments, then criticize the analyst for choosing the wrong one first.
options: Require the analyst to guess faster.
Set a shared priority order, defined outputs, and a clear route for changes.
Ask the analyst to disclose a diagnosis to justify confusion.
responses: The problem is an unresolved priority decision.
This makes management expectations usable and reviewable.
Personal disclosure is not needed to clarify conflicting instructions.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite one assignment so another person can identify its output, timing, priority, and question route.

move.control: You can explain assignments and resolve competing priorities.
move.failure: An unstated expectation is treated as an employee’s failure.

lessons.title: Respond to individual support needs without exposing them
lessons.summary: Recognize a statement that may need accommodation follow-up.
lessons.objective: Recognize a statement that may need accommodation follow-up.
objectives: Recognize a statement that may need accommodation follow-up.
Identify which information belongs in the authorized support process.
Explain a team practice without revealing an individual’s personal information.
takeaways: A request can use ordinary language.
Coordinate individual support promptly through the proper process.
Explain work arrangements without disclosing personal health information.
lessons.statement: Support the request and protect the person’s information.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Respond to individual support needs without exposing them
intro.body:
An employee does not need to recite legal terms to raise a possible accommodation need. A statement that a health condition makes a work arrangement difficult and a change is needed may require follow-up. Leaders should listen, clarify the work issue within their role, and coordinate promptly with the agency’s responsible process. They must not diagnose or request medical information or documentation from an applicant or employee seeking accommodation. Under MMB Policy 1433, any appropriate medical-information request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator. Leaders should promptly forward the request through the proper decision route rather than decide alone that it is unnecessary.

In the practice team, an analyst asks for a quieter work location because a health-related difficulty makes sustained concentration in the shared area difficult. The manager can identify the task conditions and contact the person or area responsible. The team does not need a diagnostic explanation.

Shared improvements and individual accommodations can exist together. Providing clearer written agendas for everyone does not make the quieter-location request disappear. If a support arrangement is approved, discuss its work implications without revealing the reason or promising absolute secrecy beyond the authorized process.

Identify which information belongs in the authorized support process.

How should the manager respond to coworkers’ questions?
lessons.keyStatement: Support the request and protect the person’s information.

items.title: Recognize
items.body: Listen for a requested work change connected to a health condition, even when the employee uses ordinary words. In the quieter-location case, do not require the person to say “ADA” before responding. Identify the request and involve the person or area responsible promptly rather than leaving it as an informal promise.

items.title: Coordinate
items.body: MMB Policy 1433 prohibits supervisors and managers from requesting medical information or documentation from applicants or employees seeking accommodation. Any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator; agencies must not request or accept medical records. Describe the work task and conditions, promptly forward the accommodation request to the appropriate decision maker, and explain the next-step contact.

items.title: Protect
items.body: A coworker may ask why a colleague uses a different arrangement. Explain the team’s responsibilities and that individual arrangements are handled appropriately; do not disclose a diagnosis. Fair coordination requires enough operational clarity to do the work, not a group explanation of someone’s health.

tabs.label: Private improvisation
tabs.body: An informal favor can feel responsive, but may leave the request undocumented, unsupported, or inconsistently handled. Do not use a private deal to bypass the formal process. Coordinate the request and confirm what can happen while it is being reviewed.

tabs.label: Prompt coordination
tabs.body: Prompt coordination brings the work question to people with the proper authority. It also gives the employee a clear update route. This does not guarantee the requested option; the process must consider an effective arrangement under applicable requirements.

tabs.label: Public explanation
tabs.body: Disclosing a diagnosis may seem to settle coworkers’ fairness concerns. It adds unnecessary exposure and does not establish the operational rule. Explain shared expectations and appropriate individual support without making personal health information a team discussion topic.

check.question: What should the manager do with the quieter-location request?
check.correct: Coordinate it promptly through the appropriate process while protecting personal information.
wrong: Ignore it until the employee uses a legal term.
Personally request medical information or documentation to evaluate the accommodation.
Tell the team the diagnosis to justify the arrangement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The ordinary-language request needs an appropriate response, relevant information, and privacy.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Legal vocabulary is not required to raise a possible accommodation need. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation under MMB Policy 1433; any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator. Coworkers do not need a diagnosis to understand work expectations. Promptly forward the accommodation request and protect personal information.

items.text: A health-related need for a quieter work arrangement is raised.
The supervisor contacts the person or area responsible for accommodations.
The task requires sustained review of complex figures.
The current area has frequent interruptions.
The diagnosis is posted in the team’s notes.
A supervisor requests medical documentation to evaluate an accommodation.

lessons.title: Give useful feedback and preserve development opportunity
lessons.summary: Write feedback tied to a demonstrated work requirement.
lessons.objective: Write feedback tied to a demonstrated work requirement.
objectives: Write feedback tied to a demonstrated work requirement.
Identify an opportunity restriction based on a communication assumption.
Plan development with the employee while coordinating relevant access needs.
takeaways: Use specific work evidence in feedback.
Avoid predicting development limits from a diagnosis or style.
Support access to challenging work as well as routine tasks.
lessons.statement: Clear feedback and meaningful opportunity belong together.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Give useful feedback and preserve development opportunity
intro.body:
Useful feedback identifies the work, the expectation, and what needs to happen next. It does not substitute a statement about personality, presumed disability, or cultural fit for evidence. Neuroinclusive supervision can recognize what an employee does well and address a concern without making either into a stereotype.

The practice analyst writes accurate reports but omits the recommendation in two drafts. Specific feedback names that omission and explains where the recommendation belongs. Calling the analyst “not leadership material” does not help repair the report. It also risks closing development opportunities from a limited observation.

Discuss future assignments and skills with the employee. Do not automatically reserve visible or collaborative work for staff who communicate like the manager. Where an opportunity involves a new format, examine the required function and coordinate access rather than assuming the person would not want it. Keep learning opportunities a free choice wherever the program offers them that way.

inThisLesson: Write feedback tied to a demonstrated work requirement.
Identify an opportunity restriction based on a communication assumption.
Plan development with the employee while coordinating relevant access needs.
What is the better next step?
lessons.keyStatement: Clear feedback and meaningful opportunity belong together.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: Explain the observed gap and its effect on the work. “The draft compares two options but does not state a recommendation” gives the employee an actionable task. “You are not strategic” is a broad judgment that hides the criterion and makes the response harder to evaluate.

items.title: Opportunity
items.body: A concern in one task does not establish every future limit. In the analyst case, skipping the person for a project presentation because the manager assumes discomfort removes a chance to build skill. Discuss the actual assignment, interests, expectations, and support instead.

items.title: Development
items.body: A development plan connects a desired skill to practice, feedback, and review. For example, the analyst could prepare a short recommendation and answer planned questions with relevant access arrangements. Do not frame the opportunity as a test of willingness to disclose or imitate the manager’s personal style.

tabs.label: Personality judgment
tabs.body: A personality judgment is broad and can feel conclusive, but gives little direction for improvement. It may also influence later opportunities unfairly. Replace the label with a work observation, relevant expectation, and next step that the employee can understand.

tabs.label: Specific feedback
tabs.body: Specific feedback lets the employee act and gives the leader evidence to review. It should still allow questions about instructions and work conditions. Clarity supports accountability because both people can examine whether the agreed change occurred.

tabs.label: Protective exclusion
tabs.body: Withholding challenging work may be intended as protection, yet can prevent growth and recognition. Ask about interest and needs instead of assuming them. Coordinate access and standards so the opportunity remains meaningful rather than removing the person from consideration.

check.question: Which feedback supports the analyst’s development?
check.correct: Identify the missing recommendation, explain the expected output, and plan relevant practice with feedback.
wrong: Declare the analyst unsuitable for leadership.
Remove all challenging assignments for protection.
Ask for a diagnosis before discussing development.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response makes the work expectation actionable and preserves an appropriate opportunity to learn.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A missing recommendation is a specific work gap, not proof of a permanent leadership limit. Protective exclusion can deny development, and diagnosis is not required for an ordinary skills conversation. Explain the output, invite relevant questions, and plan practice.

items.text: Identify where the recommendation is missing.
Explain how the recommendation should connect to evidence.
Discuss a supported project briefing the analyst wants to practice.
Offer feedback after the first presentation draft.
Assume all public work is unsuitable because of a label.
Treat one draft omission as a permanent inability to lead.

scenario.prompt: What is the better next step?
options: Keep the analyst permanently in routine work.
Give specific feedback and discuss a relevant development opportunity with appropriate support.
Avoid all feedback to be inclusive.
responses: The restriction exceeds the evidence and limits growth.
This addresses the concern while preserving opportunity.
Withholding useful feedback leaves the expectation unclear.

move.control: You can connect feedback and opportunities to actual work.
move.failure: An unexplained label replaces both feedback and development.

lessons.title: Review whether work conditions and opportunities improved
lessons.summary: Choose evidence that tests a particular work-design improvement.
lessons.objective: Choose evidence that tests a particular work-design improvement.
objectives: Choose evidence that tests a particular work-design improvement.
Distinguish a shared process result from an individual accommodation outcome.

takeaways: Check the result the change was meant to support.
Keep shared-process and individual-support reviews appropriately separate.

lessons.statement: A useful change needs evidence of effectiveness, not a success label.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Review whether work conditions and opportunities improved
intro.body:
After changing meeting preparation or task instructions, review the intended result. Did timely contributions reach the decision? Did staff understand which task had priority? Did the team still meet relevant accuracy and timing expectations? An improvement can support access without proving that every barrier has disappeared.

The practice team provides agendas earlier and accepts written input before policy decisions. Attendance stays the same, but written questions now identify a material evidence gap before the recommendation is finalized. That is more relevant evidence than counting how many agendas were sent. The team should also ask whether the revised process created new work or timing problems.

Individual accommodation effectiveness belongs in the appropriate private process. Do not create a diagnostic roster to explain a team result or ask employees to disclose personal information for a success story. Review development access too: better immediate task completion does not show that staff receive fair opportunities to lead or advance.

Distinguish a shared process result from an individual accommodation outcome.

What should the review use instead?
lessons.keyStatement: A useful change needs evidence of effectiveness, not a success label.

items.title: Measure
items.body: Match the evidence to the purpose. If an earlier agenda was meant to support thoughtful input, check whether useful questions reached the decision in time. The number of emails sent shows activity but not that people could contribute effectively. Preserve uncertainty about other reasons for the change.

items.title: Separate
items.body: A shared meeting improvement and an individual support arrangement have different review needs. Team feedback can examine whether instructions were clearer. A private review can consider whether a specific accommodation was effective. Combining both into a public personal story risks exposure and muddles the question.

items.title: Sustain
items.body: Keep a useful practice, adjust an ineffective one, and assign the next review. For example, retain written input but clarify its deadline if comments still arrive after decisions. Check who receives development opportunities as well; a more usable meeting does not automatically repair assignment access.

tabs.label: Activity count
tabs.body: Counting agendas confirms implementation and is easy to monitor. It does not reveal whether the timing, contents, or response route were usable. Pair it with evidence about contributions to the actual work before claiming the practice improved access.

tabs.label: Work result
tabs.body: A work result shows what happened in the process, such as a missing limitation identified before a policy recommendation. It is more informative than activity alone. Still consider other explanations and do not attribute the entire outcome to a single change.

tabs.label: Personal success story
tabs.body: A personal story can be compelling, but public praise may reveal an arrangement the employee expected to remain private. Review the process using appropriate information. Do not require someone to share a diagnosis or become the representative of neurodiversity for the team.

check.question: What best tests the earlier-agenda improvement?
check.correct: Whether useful contributions reached the decision in time, alongside relevant work outcomes and limits.
wrong: Only the number of agenda emails.
A list of staff presumed to have diagnoses.
A claim that all workplace barriers are solved.
check.feedbackCorrect: The evidence connects the change to its purpose without exposing individual information or overstating the result.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Agenda counts show activity, while guessed diagnostic lists introduce unreliable personal information. Declaring all barriers solved exceeds one process result. Check whether the actual contribution pathway improved and identify what still needs attention.

items.text: Agendas were sent earlier for four meetings.
A written-input route was added.
A material question reached the decision before closure.
Staff could identify the priority after the revised instruction.
All neurodivergent staff now have the same needs met.
One meeting change proves development opportunity is equal.

responses: The list is unnecessary and unsupported.

jobAid.subtitle: Make the work clear, examine the conditions, coordinate individual support, and review access to opportunity.
remember: A diagnosis does not predict every need or strength.
Shared improvements do not replace an individual accommodation process.
Use work evidence; do not personally request medical information or documentation for accommodation.

sections.heading: Before changing a practice
items: Name the work result and distinguish it from a familiar method.
Ask about usable work conditions without collecting diagnoses.
Identify decisions that require HR or ADA coordination.

sections.heading: During supervision
items: Give clear instructions, priorities, and specific feedback.
Respond promptly to a possible accommodation request through the established process.
Keep personal information out of team explanations and learning records.

sections.heading: When reviewing effects
items: Check whether the change supported the actual work.
Review development access as well as immediate task completion.
Retain useful shared practices and coordinate unresolved individual needs.

sources.title: JAN — Neurodiversity
sources.note: An accommodation resource describes varied individual needs and case-by-case consideration. The DHS cases in the course are examples.

sources.title: EARN — Neurodiversity in the Workplace
sources.note: ODEP-funded employer toolkit connecting recruitment, retention, management, and advancement.

sources.title: EEOC — Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship
sources.note: Federal guidance on individualized accommodation, effectiveness, requests, and confidentiality. Issued before the ADA Amendments Act; consult current requirements and agency procedures for actual decisions.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: ADA Reasonable Accommodation
sources.note: Minnesota policy, especially pages 5–7: promptly forward requests to the appropriate decision maker; supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation, and any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator. Medical records are not requested or accepted.
